definition: The zodiac sign crossing the eastern horizon at your moment of birth. It sets the whole house structure of your chart and describes the way you meet the world — which is why an accurate birth time matters so much.
A meaningful geometric angle between two planets or points in a chart, describing how their functions interact — fusing, supporting, straining, or balancing each other.
A map of the sky calculated for the exact date, time, and place of your birth, showing every planet's position by sign and house. The foundational document of Western astrology.
Shorthand for your Sun sign, Moon sign, and rising sign — the three placements most people learn first. A real chart holds far more, but these three sketch the outline.
Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn — the signs that begin each season. Cardinal energy initiates: it starts things.
A chart created from the mathematical midpoints of two people's charts, read as a portrait of the relationship itself — a third entity with its own character.
An aspect of 0°: two planets occupying the same place, blending their functions into one combined force.

The boundary line where one house or sign ends and the next begins. 'Born on the cusp' popularly refers to birthdays near a sign change — though the Sun is always in exactly one sign at any given moment.
The zodiac is a 360° circle divided into twelve 30° signs. A planet's degree pinpoints where in a sign it sits — e.g., 9°40′ Pisces.
The point opposite the Ascendant, marking the seventh-house cusp. It describes what you seek — and sometimes only recognize — in partners.

A new moon (solar eclipse) or full moon (lunar eclipse) occurring near the Moon's nodes. Astrologically, eclipses mark accelerated chapters of change along the houses they touch — significant, not sinister.
The four temperaments of the signs: Fire (spirited), Earth (practical), Air (mental), Water (feeling). Each element holds three signs.
A table of planetary positions over time — the reference astrologers use to know where everything was, is, or will be.
Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius — the signs at each season's height. Fixed energy sustains: it holds, deepens, and finishes.
The Moon opposite the Sun — maximum illumination. In practice: culminations, results coming to light, and emotional high tide. A natural review point in the lunar cycle.
The written symbol for a planet, sign, or aspect — the shorthand alphabet of a chart.

A traditional branch that answers one specific question from a chart cast for the moment the question is asked. Requires no birth data. Mo holds a Practitioner's Certificate in Horary Astrology from the School of Traditional Astrology.
One of twelve divisions of the chart representing areas of life — identity, money, communication, home, and so on. Planets act through the houses they occupy.
A method for dividing the chart into houses (Placidus, whole sign, Porphyry, and others). Astrologers differ on preference; the houses' meanings remain the same.
A planet's entry into a new sign — the start of a new tone for that planet's function, lasting until the next ingress.
The Sun and Moon — the two lights. Astrology counts them among the planets for convenience, and gives them pride of place.
A complete new-moon-to-new-moon cycle, about 29.5 days — or, loosely, any new or full moon event.
The highest point of the chart and cusp of the tenth house — your public direction: career, reputation, and what you climb toward.
How a sign moves: cardinal (initiating), fixed (sustaining), or mutable (adapting). Each modality holds four signs.
Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces — the signs that close each season. Mutable energy adapts: it distributes, adjusts, and releases.
Belonging to the birth chart. A 'natal Mars in Leo' is where Mars stood when you were born, as distinct from where it travels now.
The Moon conjunct the Sun — the dark of the moon and the seed point of a fresh lunar cycle. A natural moment for setting intentions.

The two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's apparent path. The North and South Nodes are read as a growth axis: familiar gifts (South) reaching toward unfamiliar development (North). Eclipses occur near them.
The allowance, in degrees, within which an aspect is considered active. A trine at 118° is 'in orb' by 2°. Tighter orbs, stronger aspects.

The apparent backward motion of a planet from Earth's viewpoint — an optical effect of orbital geometry, not a reversal in space. Astrologically: a season to review, revise, and reconsider that planet's themes rather than force them forward.
Everyday name for the Ascendant — the sign rising in the east at your birth.
The traditional assignment of each sign to a planetary 'ruler' whose nature it shares — Mars rules Aries, the Moon rules Cancer, and so on. Rulerships let one placement speak for another.
In traditional astrology, the day/night division of a chart. Some planets function more constructively by day (Sun, Jupiter, Saturn), others by night (Moon, Venus, Mars).
One of twelve 30° divisions of the zodiac, each lending its style of expression to planets within it.
A chart cast for the moment the Sun returns to its exact natal position each year — read as a portrait of your personal year ahead. The origin of 'many happy returns.'
The moment a planet appears to stand still before changing direction (stationing retrograde or direct). Stationing planets are considered emphatic — their themes turn up loud.
Relationship astrology's core technique: overlaying two charts to see how each person's planets aspect the other's.
The current position of a planet, especially as it forms aspects to your natal chart. Transits are the weather your chart is living through.
The pre-modern body of technique — including horary, sect, and classical rulerships — revived in recent decades. Mo works with a classical lens: traditional methods, modern conversation.
The band of sky along the Sun's apparent yearly path, divided into twelve signs. Western astrology uses the tropical zodiac, anchored to the seasons rather than the constellations.
